title: Open his eyes (2 Kings 6:15–17)
hook: the servant sees enemy armies; Elisha prays and the hills are full of fire

segments.voice: Yesterday, Naaman wanted a grand cure and got a muddy river. Your line was just wash. What simple thing did you finally do? Day seven hundred thirty-seven.

Early morning in a town called Dothan. A young man, the servant of the prophet Elisha, gets up before his master, opens the door, and steps outside. The hills around the town are covered. Horses. Chariots. A whole army from the king of Syria, sent overnight for one reason: to capture the man asleep inside. Elisha has been warning the king of Israel where the Syrians would lie in wait, not once nor twice, and the Syrian king has had enough. The servant runs back in, and the King James Bible keeps his words exactly as a frightened person says them: "Alas, my master! how shall we do?" Elisha's answer, and his prayer, are today.
screen: `ALAS, MY MASTER! HOW SHALL WE DO?`

segments.voice: Elisha doesn't say the army isn't there. It is. He says: "Fear not: for they that be with us are more than they that be with them." Hear how strange that is. Two men in a house, a cavalry outside, and he's counting, and his count comes out in their favor. Then he prays, and notice what he asks for. Not an escape. Not a fire from heaven. "LORD, I pray thee, open his eyes, that he may see." The prayer isn't for the situation to change. It's for the servant's sight to change. And it does. "The LORD opened the eyes of the young man; and he saw: and, behold, the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire round about Elisha." The fire was already there. Nothing arrived. The young man just finally saw what had been standing on the hill the whole time. Then the story turns. The Syrians come down, Elisha prays again, and this time he asks for the opposite: that the soldiers be struck blind. He leads the whole confused army into the capital, Samaria, and when their eyes open there, the king of Israel wants to strike them down. Elisha says no. Set bread and water before them. So the king throws them a great feast and sends them home to their master. The chapter says the raiding bands of Syria came no more into the land of Israel. Christians have read this scene in more than one way. Some hear it about angels, a help that is real but usually unseen. Others hear it as a picture of faith itself: not seeing new things, but seeing the same hillside differently. Either way, the hinge is a three-word prayer for someone else.
screen: `THEY THAT BE WITH US ARE MORE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look for help you haven't counted. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the thing that feels like an army on the hill right now. Let it be as big as it is. Then, slowly, start a second count. Who is on your side in this? A friend, a sister, a neighbor, a doctor, someone who prayed for you without saying so. What strength have you already got that you forgot to list? If you pray, you can borrow Elisha's words for someone else: open his eyes, or open her eyes. If you don't pray, just keep counting quietly. The bell holds the time.
Dothan. The town where Elisha's frightened servant saw the hills full of horses and chariots of fire, after a prayer: open his eyes.
Your line: more with us. Today, when something looks like it's surrounding you, stop once and count what's on your side, out loud if you can. Day seven hundred thirty-seven.

howItsDone: Some Christians turn to Elisha's servant at Dothan in frightening seasons, and some pray Elisha's request, open his eyes, for someone who is afraid; the scene is also read in churches when teaching about angels and unseen help.

original.note: Hebrew: open (the eyes), the verb of Elisha's prayer in 2 Kings 6:17.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story where angels show up to win a battle.
what it means: nothing arrives. the servant's eyes are opened to what was already on the hill, and the battle ends in a feast.
what a scholar hears: Elisha prays the same verb twice in opposite directions: open the servant's eyes (6:17), then the soldiers' eyes in Samaria (6:20).

notes: Spoken quotation of 6:17 omits 'and said' and joins the prayer and the answer; the sources entry gives the KJV words used. Confirm the spoken splice is acceptable.
Blinding, leading to Samaria, the feast and 'the bands of Syria came no more' are summarized from 6:18–23. Confirm the paraphrase.
Day 735 (The chariot of fire, 2 Kings 2) also has chariots of fire; this day's angle is sight, not departure. Check the two days don't overlap in the writer of 735's version.
Two readings (angels as unseen help; faith as seeing the same scene differently) attributed to 'Christians... in more than one way'; confirm fair.
Trapdoor floor 3: confirm 6:17 and 6:20 use the same Hebrew verb (פקח).
Original: פְּקַח (imperative, 'open'); in the verse it is פְּקַח־נָא אֶת־עֵינָיו. Confirm pointing and pronunciation.
Editor pass: cut 'small' (Dothan's size is not in the text); 'every Syrian ambush' changed to the text's 'not once nor twice' (6:10); stock line 'a turn nobody expects' cut.
